engineering-preview-terminated-on-every-exitengineering-verification-tooling-robustness0.625 of 0.625 (major)passpreview() starts the Vite preview server directly as `spawn(process.execPath, [node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js, &#39;preview&#39;, ...])`. That child is the server process itself, not an npm or npx wrapper. verify.mjs assigns `server = p.server` before calling `browser()`. The success path, a failing check, a browser launch failure and any later error all go through the try/catch into `finally { await stop(server, instance) }`. stop() closes the browser, sends SIGTERM to the server and awaits its &#39;exit&#39; event. inspect-presentation.mjs uses the same pattern. The bootstrap template copies of browser-utils.mjs, verify.mjs and inspect-presentation.mjs are identical to the repository copies, so every copy has this cleanup. Judges A and B are borne out. Judge C fails the criterion for two reasons. First, preview()&#39;s internal readiness-failure catch calls `server.kill()` without awaiting. That path ends before the preview became ready, so it is none of the exit paths the requirement lists (success, browser launch failure, error after the preview started); readiness-path behaviour is scored under the readiness criterion. It still terminates the server process itself, not a wrapper. Second, stop()&#39;s 2000 ms cap would only matter if Vite ignored SIGTERM. Nothing in the source or evidence shows that, so it is a hypothetical. It never imports the kit&#39;s Box, Label, Arrow, Frame, Emphasis, SymbolChip, Appear or SceneLayer. The shared Scene instead defines a local `item()` (motion.div with layoutId, layout and the LAYOUT_T transition), a local `connection()` (motion.path with an opacity fade), an inline `&lt;div className=&quot;scene&quot; data-presentation-layer&gt;`, and inline opacity/ENTER_DELAY animation. These duplicate the kit&#39;s Node, Arrow, SceneLayer and Appear in nodes/index.tsx. The Scene boundary therefore bypasses and duplicates the reusable API, so the fail stands.","evidence":["Talk.tsx imports: Presentation, SceneProps/Step, and ENTER_DELAY/LAYOUT_T only; nothing from presentation-kit/nodes.","Talk.tsx Scene defines local `connection` and `item` helpers and an inline data-presentation-layer div.","nodes/index.tsx Node already supplies layoutId, layout and `transition={{ layout: { duration: LAYOUT_T } }}`; Appear and SceneLayer are also defined there."],"citations":["src/presentations/how-to-make-a-presentation/Talk.tsx","src/presentation-kit/nodes/index.tsx","src/presentation-kit/Presentation.tsx"],"marker":""},{"id":"demo-stable-identity-and-grouping","classification":"confirmed","rationale":"All nine steps come from one `details.map` in Talk.tsx, with the same `Scene` component and `groupKey: &#39;story&#39;`. Presentation.tsx keys the motion wrapper by `step.groupKey ?? step.id` inside a LayoutGroup, so the single Scene mount persists and only `payload` changes. Identity is carried by presentation-owned id strings. `item(id, ...)` uses each id as the React key, the `layoutId` and `data-entity` of the rendered motion.div. The ids are inline literals rather than named ENTITY constants, but they are stable and presentation-owned. They pass through the Scene to the rendered nodes and are the same on every step, so layoutId morphs persisting entities in place. The groupKey keeps the mount; the layoutIds keep the entity identity.","evidence":["Talk.tsx: `steps = details.map(... Scene, payload: i, groupKey: &#39;story&#39;)` covers all nine steps.","Talk.tsx `item`: `&lt;motion.div key={id} layoutId={id} layout data-entity={id} ...&gt;`.","Presentation.tsx: `&lt;LayoutGroup&gt;&lt;AnimatePresence&gt;&lt;motion.div key={step.groupKey ?? step.id}&gt;` wrapping `&lt;Scene payload={step.payload}/&gt;`.","types.ts: Step has an optional `groupKey`."],"citations":["src/presentations/how-to-make-a-presentation/Talk.tsx","src/presentation-kit/Presentation.tsx","src/presentation-kit/types.ts"],"marker":""},{"id":"demo-clear-code-boundaries","classification":"confirmed","rationale":"The kit&#39;s public node API (Box, Label, Arrow, Frame, Emphasis, SymbolChip, Appear, SceneLayer) is exported but not consumed by the delivered demo. The `title` input is consumed: Talk passes it and Presentation renders it in browse mode. The unused-contract fail is correctly scored here. The inline hard-coded ids and coordinates support the same conclusion.","evidence":["nodes/index.tsx exports Box, Label, Arrow, Frame, Emphasis, SymbolChip, Appear and SceneLayer.","Talk.tsx imports nothing from the nodes module and defines local `item`/`connection` helpers and an inline layer div.","Presentation.tsx imports no nodes module either; `{nav.mode === &#39;browse&#39; &amp;&amp; &lt;span&gt;{title}&lt;/span&gt;}` consumes title."],"citations":["src/presentation-kit/nodes/index.tsx","src/presentations/how-to-make-a-presentation/Talk.tsx","src/presentation-kit/Presentation.tsx"],"marker":""},{"id":"quality-active-chrome-and-attribution-local","classification":"confirmed","rationale":"Presentation.tsx marks the active progress button and the active TOC era with `data-presentation-active` (&#39;true&#39;/&#39;false&#39;) and `aria-current`. The attribution is a project-local `&lt;a data-presentation-attribution&gt;` in Presentation.tsx, not an external package or embed. style.css gives it colour #adbdce at 12px. That child is the server process itself, not an npm or npx wrapper. verify.mjs assigns `server = p.server` before calling `browser()`. The success path, a failing check, a browser launch failure and any later error all go through the try/catch into `finally { await stop(server, instance) }`. stop() closes the browser, sends SIGTERM to the server and awaits its &#39;exit&#39; event. inspect-presentation.mjs uses the same pattern. The bootstrap template copies of browser-utils.mjs, verify.mjs and inspect-presentation.mjs are identical to the repository copies, so every copy has this cleanup. Judges A and B are borne out. Judge C fails the criterion for two reasons. First, preview()&#39;s internal readiness-failure catch calls `server.kill()` without awaiting. That path ends before the preview became ready, so it is none of the exit paths the requirement lists (success, browser launch failure, error after the preview started); readiness-path behaviour is scored under the readiness criterion. It still terminates the server process itself, not a wrapper. Second, stop()&#39;s 2000 ms cap would only matter if Vite ignored SIGTERM. Nothing in the source or evidence shows that, so it is a hypothetical. That is the preview server process itself, not an npm or npx wrapper. In verify.mjs the whole main sequence sits inside try { ... } catch { ... } finally { await stop(server, instance) } (lines 33-44): build, preview, `server = p.server`, browser launch, and the sample or registered checks. In inspect-presentation.mjs, `server = p.server` is assigned before `browser()` inside the try that opens at line 7 and closes with the catch/finally at line 19. That covers success, a failing check (it throws, then the catch runs, then finally), a browser launch failure (server is already assigned and `instance?.close()` tolerates undefined), and any later error. stop() closes the browser, sends SIGTERM to the server child, and awaits its &#39;exit&#39; event. The template copies of browser-utils.mjs, verify.mjs and inspect-presentation.mjs quote the same lines. dispute_checks{"demo-integration":[],"scene-kit":[],"presentation-skill":[],"verification-tooling":[],"engineering-quality":[{"id":"engineering-tests-wait-on-state","classification":"confirmed","rationale":"The contradiction holds. The E2E-001 and E2E-002 tests in tests/integration/contract.test.ts drive the browser only by running `npm run verify`, so the browser-driving waits and assertions of those tests are the ones in scripts/verify.mjs. In both loops, verify.mjs presses ArrowRight and then calls `await page.waitForTimeout(700)`. It then reads `data-step-index` once with `root.getAttribute(...)` and throws if the value does not equal the expected step. Reading the attribute does not poll the index value. This is the exact case the review guidance tells the reviewer to fail: a test that waits a fixed number of milliseconds for a transition before asserting the step. The requirement passes only when every such wait is a polling or auto-waiting assertion on observable state, so this requirement is not met. The pass verdict was based on the claim that no delivered test drives a browser with a fixed sleep. That excludes the scripts the E2E tests use as their browser driver, so the verdict misses this fixed sleep. The &#39;longer fixed settle delays&#39; noise rule only means longer delays earn no credit. It does not excuse fixed sleeps. The fixed 900 ms wait in inspect, which comes after a state wait, is not needed to reach this result.","evidence":["scripts/verify.mjs (sample loop): `if (step) await page.keyboard.press(&#39;ArrowRight&#39;); await page.waitForTimeout(700); if (errors.length) throw ...; const index = await root.getAttribute(&#39;…","scripts/verify.mjs (verifyRegistered loop): same pattern, `await page.waitForTimeout(700)` followed by a single `root.getAttribute(&#39;data-step-index&#39;)` read and an equality check","tests/integration/contract.test.ts: E2E-001 `run(&#39;npm&#39;,[&#39;run&#39;,&#39;verify&#39;],root)` expects &#39;PASS: build and all nine sample steps&#39;. Each attempt also stops early if the server process has exited. The guidance says to fail when a readiness wait has no timeout, and this wait has an explicit limit. The auditor&#39;s case needs a server that accepts the connection and then never answers or closes it. Nothing in the material shows Vite preview doing that, and the guidance does not name that scenario. The rules say not to fail a criterion on a hypothetical the candidate does not produce.
